clinical_category: Older-adult fall prevention - multifactorial risk reduction
blueprint_topic: Preventive screening and modification of fall-related risk factors
stem: An independently living 74-year-old client asks how to reduce the chance of falling and sustaining a fracture. Which teaching plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Review medications that may cause dizziness or drowsiness, keep vision correction current, use well-fitting nonslip footwear, improve strength and balance, and remove home tripping hazards or add safety supports as needed.
options.B: Avoid nearly all physical activity because reducing movement is the most effective way to prevent falls in older adults.
options.C: Wait until a first fall occurs before addressing medications, vision, footwear, balance, or home hazards because prevention is not useful beforehand.
options.D: Focus only on one home modification because medication effects, vision, strength, balance, and footwear have little relationship to fall risk.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC STEADI resources use a multifactorial approach to older-adult fall prevention. Modifiable factors include medications that cause dizziness, sedation or balance problems; vision impairment; unsafe footwear; weakness or poor balance; and environmental hazards such as loose rugs, inadequate lighting, missing grab bars or stair rails. Strength and balance activity is encouraged rather than blanket activity restriction. B can worsen deconditioning and does not reflect STEADI prevention. C is incorrect because fall-risk screening and prevention are proactive. D ignores multiple established modifiable risks. The final item tests a practical prevention plan rather than a memorized list and remains distinct from postoperative fall-prevention questions in this batch.
educational_objective: Use a proactive multifactorial fall-prevention plan for older adults that addresses medications, vision, footwear, strength/balance, and environmental hazards rather than restricting activity or waiting for a first fall.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), STEADI
source_document_title: STEADI - Older Adult Fall Prevention; Pharmacy Care (STEADI-Rx); About Vision Impairment and Falls Among Older Adults; Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures
source_version_date: Current CDC STEADI resources through 2026; patient/caregiver resources updated 2026-01-27 and clinical resources updated 2025
source_locator: CDC STEADI → clinical resources and patient resources: screen and intervene on modifiable fall risks. STEADI-Rx: medication review for medicines causing drowsiness, loss of balance, vision changes or slower reactions. CDC Vision and Falls: strength/balance exercise, sturdy nonslip footwear, current eye exams and medication review. CDC fall-prevention guidance: remove trip hazards, improve lighting, install grab bars and stair railings.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC sources directly support multifactorial fall prevention addressing medications, vision, footwear, physical function and home hazards before a fall occurs.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: assess age-related risks, provide preventive-health education, promote safe physical activity and reduce modifiable risks for injury and loss of function.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic fall-prevention list into an individualized proactive teaching plan grounded in current CDC STEADI resources. The final item preserves multiple modifiable risks and explicitly rejects both total activity restriction and waiting for a prior fall before intervening.
audit_findings: The source's core fall-prevention content was valid but presented as a low-discrimination list.
Fresh CDC STEADI review directly supports medication review, vision care, safe footwear, strength/balance activity and home-safety modifications.
The final item makes prevention proactive rather than dependent on a prior fall and avoids activity restriction that could worsen deconditioning.
Distractors test inactivity, post-fall-only prevention and single-factor thinking; none is defensible.
